headline: Megaspeed Listing Puts New Transactions Behind a Licence Gate
deck: A final rule places seven entities under a presumptive-denial licensing rule, while qualifying cargo already in transit retains a 30-day path.
body: The Federal Register’s public-inspection system filed BIS final rule 2026-23999, adding seven entities in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand to the Entity List, with publication scheduled for Nov. 25 [E1][E2]. The rule requires licences for all items subject to the Export Administration Regulations and says applications will be reviewed under a presumption of denial [E3].

On Nov. 19, the paper reported that House Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie had requested briefings from Nvidia and Commerce officials about Megaspeed and national-security concerns [E7]. What changed is a formal transaction-level licensing rule, rather than congressional requests for information.

A savings clause allows shipments already en route to proceed under their former eligibility if they are completed within 30 days of public inspection [E4]. The Justice Department has taken the lead in a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, while Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing and said it complies with U.S. export-control rules [E5][E6].

**The desk's reading.** The listing is an export-control gate: suppliers, reexporters and transferors now need a licence before dealing in covered items with the named entities, and the stated review posture makes approval uncertain. It does not establish that all shipments have stopped, because qualifying in-transit cargo has a stated exception and the rule says nothing here about the outcome of individual licence applications or a criminal case.

**The next test.** The practical effect will become visible in licence decisions, exporters' shipment records or evidence of cargo completing under the 30-day savings clause after public inspection. Those records would distinguish a broad interruption from a rule whose immediate effect is confined to new transactions.
